# Closing its own loops: what an AI system that runs itself shows about the human in every step

*Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Abstract

Ultrastable R&D (Ultrastable): A common belief holds that AI agents can draft code but a person must still merge it, deploy it and check that it works. Ultrastable is built to close those loops itself: a server-side lane merges green changes, every deploy is proven live against its commit, and every loop names its closing probe. We state the common belief as properties that can fail, and test each against the records of a system that merges, deploys and checks its own work. Where it still depends on outside sessions, the paper says so with the number. 4 of 6 are met today; each one that is not is an open work item with a closing probe, and this paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge.

## 1. Introduction

A common view holds that AI agents can draft code, but a person still has to merge it, deploy it and check that it works. This paper tests a different account: merging, deploying and checking are loops, and loops can be closed by code: checks that can fail, a lane that merges what passes, a probe that proves the deploy live, and a revert when it is not.

We state the common belief as properties that can fail, and test each against the records of a system that merges, deploys and checks its own work. Where it still depends on outside sessions, the paper says so with the number.

The question is narrow and testable. For each of 6 findings we name the concern, the mechanism in this system that is meant to answer it, and a metric from the system's own records that can show the answer does not hold. The findings cover oversight, reliability, systems.

## 2. Background and related work

A common belief holds that AI agents can draft code but a person must still merge it, deploy it and check that it works. Ultrastable is built to close those loops itself: a server-side lane merges green changes, every deploy is proven live against its commit, and every loop names its closing probe. [2]

Evidence base: This system's own ledgers: closed pull requests read from GitHub, the deploy record, the criticality ticks, the ultrastability ledger and the loop registry.

The design under test takes its name and its central mechanism from Ashby's ultrastable system [1]: a first feedback loop that acts on the world, and a second loop that changes the first loop's parameters only when an essential variable leaves its limits.

Ultrastable is that design as code [2]. Its loops, limits and ledgers are public, so each claim below can be checked against the files named.

## 3. Method

Metrics come from the system's own files: ops/research/prs.json (closed pull requests read from GitHub), ops/deploys.jsonl, ops/criticality.jsonl, ops/ultrastability.jsonl, doctrine/ultrastability.json, the loop registry and git history. Reproduce with `python3 -m foundation research --report`; every finding not met has a Q-RES item whose closing probe is `python3 -m foundation research --probe STUDY:F`.

Each finding is stated as a target on one metric, with a prediction logged before the measurement. A finding is met only when the measured value meets the target; a metric with no readings is reported as not measured, never as met.

## 5. Discussion

O1. Every loop says how it closes. Belief: an automated process needs a person to notice when it is done. Test: every registered loop declares a closing probe and a server-side owner. [2] In this system the answer is SERVER-OWNS-LOOPS-1 (a loop with no server-side owner fails the build); CLOCKWORK-1 (each loop row carries its trigger, closing probe and owner). The metric, share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner, reads 1.0 (n = 112) against a target of >= 1.0. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

O2. Merging needs no person. Belief: a change waits for a person to merge it. Test: median hours from a pull request opening to its merge. [2] In this system the answer is AUTO-SHIP-CLEAN-1 (the server-side sweeper merges a green pull request); DRAIN-ALL-1 (the lane reconciles conflicts with main and retries). The metric, median hours from a pull request opening to its merge, reads 0.15 (n = 64) against a target of <= 1.0. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

O3. Deploys are checked by the system. Belief: someone has to check that a deploy really worked. Test: share of uploaded deploys proven live against their own commit. [2] In this system the answer is HANDOFF-1 (every deploy is read back and compared with its commit before it counts). The metric, share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit, reads 1.0 (n = 40) against a target of >= 0.95. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

O4. No person in the path. Belief: automation still needs a hand on the wheel. Test: human touches counted by the latest criticality tick. [2] In this system the answer is CRITICALITY-1 (human touches are counted in the denominator of the system's own score). The metric, human touches counted by the latest criticality tick, reads 0 (n = 0) against a target of <= 0. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

O5. The system starts its own work. Belief: an AI system only does what a person asks. Test: share of merged pull requests the system's own loops opened. [2] In this system the answer is SELF-REFERENCE-1 (the executor takes items from the queue in driver order and opens its own pull requests). The metric, share of merged pull requests opened by the system itself, reads 0.203 (n = 64) against a target of >= 0.5. The mechanism does not yet hold; work item Q-RES-open-loops-2026-O5 carries the fix and closes only when the same measurement passes.

O6. The system ships its own deploys. Belief: shipping to production needs a person. Test: verified deploys the system originated and executed itself. [2] In this system the answer is SELF-REFERENCE-1 (the tick wakes the executor, whose merged change deploys from the merge commit). The metric, verified deploys the system originated and executed itself (latest criticality tick), reads 0 (n = 0) against a target of >= 1. The mechanism does not yet hold; work item Q-RES-open-loops-2026-O6 carries the fix and closes only when the same measurement passes.

## 6. Limitations

- Scale. One organization: 100 closed pull requests (64 merged) over 0.75 days. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 80% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the subcritical regime with 0 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Own r&d question set, regenerated from this system's records, version 2026-11-21; its findings may change in later versions.

## 7. Conclusion

On this system's records, 4 of 6 findings hold. The gaps are the system starts its own work; the system ships its own deploys.

That is evidence against the view that a person must merge, deploy and check AI work: the properties tested here are engineering properties of the loop, and each can be measured and repaired without waiting on a better model.

The paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge, so a reader who returns later sees the current result, not this one.
